title: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
summary: How the operators that dominate vision preprocessing are written for a GPU: layout and pitch, the exact interpolation arithmetic, inverse maps and borders, color matrices, tiled convolution and batching.
outcomes: Explain why NHWC or NCHW and the row pitch decide whether a per-pixel kernel's loads coalesce
Compute bilinear and nearest resize outputs with the half-pixel center convention, and the shift an off-by-half causes
Explain warp as an inverse map and pick a border rule, predicting the index each rule fetches
Compute a BT.601 luma value in float and in CV-CUDA's 14-bit fixed point, and say why BT.709 gives a different answer
Compute how many extra loads a shared-memory halo adds and when one batched launch beats per-image launches

lessons.title: Pixels in memory: NHWC, NCHW, pitch and a warp's 96 bytes

blocks.md:
A vision pipeline in front of a model does the same four things to every frame: decode, resize, convert color, normalize into the tensor the network wants. Each of those steps touches every pixel once and does a handful of arithmetic operations on it. That makes them bandwidth problems, not math problems, so the first thing that decides their speed is not the interpolation formula but where the bytes are.

Two layouts dominate. In **NHWC** (also called interleaved or packed) a pixel's channels sit next to each other: R, G, B, R, G, B. In **NCHW** (planar) each channel is a full image of its own: all the reds, then all the greens, then all the blues. CV-CUDA names both as tensor layouts, where N is the batch index, H height, W width and C channels.

blocks.tex: \text{NHWC: } \text{off} = n\,S_n + y\,S_y + x\,C + c \qquad \text{NCHW: } \text{off} = n\,S_n + c\,S_c + y\,S_y + x
blocks.caption: Byte offsets for an 8-bit image. The strides S are stored per dimension, not derived from the width, which is what lets a row be padded.

blocks.md:
That padding is the **pitch**: the number of bytes from the start of one row to the start of the next, which can be larger than the row's useful bytes. A 1021-pixel-wide RGB8 row holds 3063 useful bytes; padded to a 32-byte boundary the pitch becomes 3072, nine bytes of waste per row that buy every row the same alignment as the first. CV-CUDA exposes this directly: `cvcuda.Image((1920, 1080), cvcuda.Format.RGB8, rowalign=32)` aligns rows to 32-byte boundaries. The CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide says memory from `cudaMalloc()` is "guaranteed to be aligned to at least 256 bytes", so row zero always starts well aligned; pitch is what extends that promise to row 7.

Always index with the stored stride, never with `width * channels`. A kernel that assumes the two are equal reads the padding as if it were pixels and shears the image by a few pixels per row.

blocks.title: The same four pixels, two layouts, one warp

scenes.caption: One row of four RGB8 pixels, 12 bytes either way. NHWC keeps a pixel's three channels adjacent; NCHW keeps a channel's pixels adjacent. The bytes are identical, only the order differs.

Lane 0 of a warp handles pixel 0. In NHWC its three channels are bytes 0, 1, 2, one short contiguous run. In NCHW they are bytes 0, 4, 8, one in each plane, three separate streams that are 4 bytes apart here and H times W bytes apart in a real image.

Now look at one instruction instead of one lane. The load that fetches the red channel runs in all four lanes at once. In NHWC those addresses are 3 bytes apart; in NCHW they are 1 byte apart, the fully coalesced case.

A full warp of 32 lanes, one pixel each, spans 96 bytes of NHWC: three 32-byte sectors. The warp's footprint is contiguous, so nothing is wasted overall, but each single-byte load instruction uses only 32 of the 96 bytes its sectors carry.

blocks.md:
The fix is not to change layout but to widen the access. CV-CUDA's color conversion source makes the point exactly: "a uchar3 has alignment 1, so one RGB8 pixel is three 1-byte accesses. A four-pixel carrier moves the same bytes in three 4-byte accesses, or one 16-byte access for RGBA8 - a quarter of the memory instructions". Counting for 32 pixels: 96 single-byte accesses for the naive uchar3 kernel, 24 four-byte accesses for the carrier, 32 four-byte accesses if the format is RGBA8 and each lane loads a whole pixel at once.

Its resize operator tunes the block shape for the same reason. The var-shape dispatch, the path for a batch of differently sized images, comments that "A warp row spans BLOCK_WIDTH * sizeof(T) bytes of the output", so for a 1-byte single-channel image a block 8 columns wide covers only 8 bytes of a row and the kernel goes "L1/TEX-throughput bound"; the code widens that case to 32 columns so a warp row covers a whole 32-byte sector.

blocks.title: Memory instructions per 32 pixels, same bytes moved

scenes.caption: Three ways for a warp to read 32 pixels. The naive uchar3 kernel issues 3 single-byte loads per lane. A carrier spanning four pixels moves the same 96 bytes in 4-byte chunks. An RGBA8 pixel is one aligned 4-byte load.

The same three in bytes fetched per byte used by the instruction. The byte-load kernel pulls 96 bytes of sectors to use 32 of them; the wide accesses use everything. Simplified: L1 hits make the waste cheaper than this ratio.

blocks.md: For a per-pixel operator, layout plus pitch decides how wide an aligned access each lane can make. NHWC gives a pixel's channels locality and lets one load carry a whole pixel when channels are padded to 4; NCHW gives each channel a unit-stride stream. Neither is wrong, and both lose if the kernel accesses one byte at a time.

blocks.question: A color-convert kernel reads an RGB8 (uchar3) NHWC image with one pixel per thread. Why is the per-instruction load efficiency about 33 percent?
options: The image rows are not padded, so the second row starts unaligned
Each channel load has stride 3 across lanes, so its sectors carry three times the bytes that one instruction uses
NHWC always loses to NCHW because planes are contiguous
A warp of 32 threads cannot cover 96 bytes in fewer than 32 transactions
blocks.explain: A uchar3 has alignment 1, so a pixel is three separate 1-byte accesses. Each of those instructions touches 32 addresses that are 3 bytes apart, spanning 96 bytes of sectors to deliver 32 useful bytes. The warp's total footprint is still contiguous, which is why the fix is a wider access (a 4-pixel carrier or an RGBA8 format), not a different layout.

blocks.question: An RGB8 image is 1021 pixels wide with rows padded to 32 bytes, so the pitch is 3072. What is the byte offset of the green channel of pixel (x = 5, y = 7)?
blocks.explain: Offset is y times pitch plus x times channels plus c: 7 x 3072 = 21504, plus 5 x 3 = 15, plus c = 1, giving 21520. Using width times channels (3063) instead of the pitch would give 21457, which lands 63 bytes earlier, near the end of row 6: that is the shear a kernel shows when it ignores the stored stride.

lessons.title: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row

blocks.md:
Resize is written as a **gather**: one thread owns one output pixel, works out where that output pixel came from in the source, and reads the taps it needs. The whole operator is therefore one question, asked once per output pixel: given output index $x_d$, what is the source coordinate $x_s$?

The naive answer, $x_s = x_d \cdot s$ with $s = W_{src}/W_{dst}$, treats a pixel as a point at integer coordinates. The convention production libraries have converged on treats a pixel as a little square whose **center** sits at integer coordinates, so the mapping runs center to center.

blocks.caption: The half-pixel center convention. Add a half to reach the output pixel's center, scale into source units, subtract a half to get back to source pixel indices.

blocks.md: This is exactly what the code does. CV-CUDA's bilinear resize computes `float fy = (float)((dst_y + 0.5f) * scale_y - 0.5f)` and the same for x, then takes `sx = floor(fx)` and uses the fractional part as the weight. NVIDIA's NPP documents the same thing for its ResizeSqrPixel functions, in a different algebra: with `nAdjustedXFactor = 1.0 / nXFactor` and `nAdjustedXShift = nXShift * nAdjustedXFactor + ((1.0 - nAdjustedXFactor) * 0.5)`, it sets `nSrcX = nAdjustedXFactor * nDstX - nAdjustedXShift`. With no extra shift requested, expand it: $s\,x_d - (1-s)/2 = s(x_d + 1/2) - 1/2$. Same formula. NPP's prose for it is that the functions "attempt to choose source pixels that would approximately represent the center of the destination pixels".

blocks.title: Upscaling a 4-pixel row to 8 with bilinear weights

scenes.caption: Source row of four 8-bit values, output row of eight. The scale is s = 4/8 = 0.5, so every output pixel asks for a source coordinate half a step apart.
Output 0 maps to x_s = (0 + 0.5) x 0.5 - 0.5 = -0.25, which is outside the source. CV-CUDA clamps the index to 0 and forces the weight to 0, so the output is simply source[0] = 10.
Output 1 maps to x_s = 0.25: floor gives index 0, the fractional part 0.25 is the weight on the right tap, so the value is 0.75 x 10 + 0.25 x 40 = 17.5.
Output 2 maps to 0.75, the same pair of taps with the weights swapped: 0.25 x 10 + 0.75 x 40 = 32.5. Each source interval of one pixel feeds exactly two outputs at 2x upscale.
The whole row. Outputs 3 to 6 interpolate inside the source; output 7 maps to 3.25, past the last center, where the index is clamped to 2 and the weight forced to 1, so it returns source[3] = 160.
Drop the two halves and the same eight outputs become 10, 25, 40, 65, 90, 125, 160, 160. The image slides left by half an output pixel and the last two outputs are now duplicates of the edge.

blocks.prompt: Now downscale the same row by 2, from 4 pixels to 2, with bilinear interpolation and half-pixel centers. What are the two output values, and what do the weights turn out to be?
blocks.reveal:
With $s = 2$, $x_s = 2x_d + 0.5$, so output 0 reads coordinate 0.5 and output 1 reads 2.5. Both have fractional part 0.5 exactly, so each output is the plain average of two neighbours: 25 and 125.

That is not a coincidence of this row. At an exact 2x downscale every output lands on a half-integer, which is why CV-CUDA ships a specialized kernel for it whose comment reads "At src == 2*dst every output has srcCoord = 2*dst + 0.5" and whose weights are hard-coded to `float2{0.5f, 0.5f}`. In two dimensions that makes bilinear-at-exactly-2x identical to a 2x2 box average.

blocks.title: A 4x4 image to 2x2: averaging versus decimation

scenes.caption: The 4x4 source. We want a 2x2 output, so s = 2 on both axes and every output coordinate is a half-integer.
Output (0,0) maps to source (0.5, 0.5). All four bilinear weights are 0.25, so it is the average of the top-left 2x2 block: (10 + 40 + 20 + 50) / 4 = 30.
Output (0,1) maps to (2.5, 0.5) and averages the next block: (90 + 160 + 100 + 170) / 4 = 130. The four outputs come out as 30, 130 on the first row and 50, 150 on the second.

Without the half-pixel term every output coordinate is an exact integer, all the weight lands on one tap, and bilinear collapses into decimation: the outputs are 10, 90 and 30, 110. That is where downscaling aliasing comes from.

blocks.md:
Nearest neighbour has the same choice and the same trap. CV-CUDA computes `sy = min(floor((dst_y + 0.5f) * scale_y), height - 1)` for `NVCV_INTERP_NEAREST` and drops the offset for `NVCV_INTERP_NEAREST_FLOOR`. On our row, 4 down to 2, the half-pixel version picks source indices 1 and 3 (values 40 and 160); the floor version picks 0 and 2 (values 10 and 90). A whole source pixel of difference, from one missing constant.

How big is the error in general? Subtract the two formulas: the naive coordinate is short of the correct one by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, independent of position. It is zero only at $s = 1$. Resizing 1920 wide down to 224 means $s = 8.571$ and a shift of 3.79 source pixels, which is why a detector trained on one preprocessing stack can lose accuracy when inference uses the other.

blocks.title: Shift from dropping the half-pixel term

scenes.caption: From a 1920-wide source, the error measured in source pixels grows without bound as the output gets smaller: 3.79 source pixels at the common 224-wide crop, and zero only when the output width equals the source width.
In output pixels the same error saturates just under half a pixel, which is why the bug is easy to miss by eye on a thumbnail and still moves every box coordinate a detector regresses.

Raise the source to 4096 wide and both curves rise: the same output size now needs a bigger scale factor, so the same missing constant costs more. Upscaling (output wider than source) flips the sign and shifts the other way.

blocks.md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

blocks.question: You resize a 4-pixel row to 2 pixels with nearest neighbour. Which source indices does the half-pixel convention read, and which does the floor convention read?
options: Both read 0 and 2, because floor of a half-integer rounds down
Half-pixel reads 1 and 3; floor reads 0 and 2
Half-pixel reads 0 and 2; floor reads 1 and 3
Both read 1 and 3, because the half is added before scaling
blocks.explain: Half-pixel: floor((0 + 0.5) x 2) = 1 and floor((1 + 0.5) x 2) = 3. Floor convention: 0 x 2 = 0 and 1 x 2 = 2. At this scale the two conventions never agree on a single pixel, and the half-pixel one reads the source pixel that covers the output pixel's center.

blocks.question: Dropping the minus one half from the source coordinate produces a shift of (s - 1) / 2 source pixels. When is that shift exactly zero?
options: When the output is larger than the source
Only when s = 1, that is when the output size equals the source size
When s is an integer, because the taps land on pixel centers
When nearest neighbour is used instead of bilinear
blocks.explain: The expression (s - 1) / 2 vanishes only at s = 1. Integer scale factors are the worst case for visibility, not the safe case: at s = 2 the shift is half a source pixel and at s = 4 it is 1.5 source pixels. Upscaling gives a negative shift, not zero.

lessons.title: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule

blocks.md:
A warp moves pixels to new positions: rotate, shear, scale, or the general projective map used to undo a camera's perspective. The obvious implementation is to walk the source pixels and write each one where the transform sends it. That is a **scatter**, and it fails twice over: two source pixels can round to the same destination (a write conflict between threads) and some destinations get no writes at all (holes).

Take a 4x4 image rotated 30 degrees about its center. Round each of the 16 source pixels to the nearest destination: they land on 16 distinct cells, but only 12 of those fall inside the 4x4 output. Four destination pixels inside the grid are never touched, and no amount of extra threads fills them, because the holes are a property of the map, not of the schedule.

blocks.prompt: So the kernel runs the other way: one thread per destination pixel, pulling from the source. What does the kernel need in order to do that, given a transform written as the usual 2x3 matrix that maps source to destination?
blocks.reveal:
It needs the **inverse** of that matrix. Gathering means asking "which source coordinate landed on me", so the kernel evaluates the destination-to-source map.

This is why the API and the kernel disagree about direction, and both sides document it. NPP describes its affine coefficients forward: "A pixel location (x, y) in the source image is mapped to (x', y') in the destination image." CV-CUDA takes that forward matrix and inverts it on the device, one thread per image, in `inverseMatWarpAffine`, unless the caller passes `NVCV_WARP_INVERSE_MAP`, in which case "the caller's six coefficients are the destination-to-source map itself".

blocks.tex: \begin{bmatrix} x_s \\ y_s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} m_0 & m_1 & m_2 \\ m_3 & m_4 & m_5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_d \\ y_d \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
blocks.caption: What the kernel evaluates per output pixel: six coefficients, two fused multiply-adds each, giving a fractional source coordinate that then goes through the same interpolation as resize.
Four FMAs per pixel for affine. The six coefficients are the same for every pixel, so the kernel stages them in shared memory once per block rather than re-reading them.

blocks.md: Rotating our 4x4 by 30 degrees about its center gives the forward matrix with rows $(0.866, -0.5, 0.951)$ and $(0.5, 0.866, -0.549)$. Inverting it gives the map the kernel actually runs: rows $(0.866, 0.5, -0.549)$ and $(-0.5, 0.866, 0.951)$. Destination $(1,1)$ pulls from source $(0.817, 1.317)$, comfortably inside. Destination $(0,0)$ pulls from $(-0.549, 0.951)$, which is outside the image, and so do 7 others: half of this tiny output has no source to read.

blocks.title: Which destination pixels fall off the source

scenes.caption: The source x coordinate the inverse map produces for each of the 16 destination pixels of a 30 degree rotation. Values below 0 or above 3 are outside the 4-pixel-wide source.
The source y coordinates for the same 16 pixels. A rotation mixes the axes, so a destination pixel can be inside on one axis and outside on the other.

Marking 1 where either coordinate leaves the source: 8 of 16 destination pixels need a border rule. Rotating a rectangle into a rectangle always does this, which is why warp takes a border mode and resize usually does not.

blocks.md: A border rule turns an out-of-range index into something readable. CV-CUDA's `NVCVBorderType` lists `NVCV_BORDER_CONSTANT` ("Uses a constant value for borders"), `REPLICATE` ("Replicates the last element"), `REFLECT` ("Reflects the border elements"), `WRAP` ("Wraps the border elements"), `REFLECT101` ("Reflects the border elements, excluding the last element") and `CONSTANT_COVERAGE`, which blends the constant in by how much of the interpolation window fell outside. Other libraries use overlapping names: NPP has CONSTANT, REPLICATE and WRAP but calls its reflecting modes MIRROR and MIRROR_REFL. The rules differ only in how they fold an index back, and the difference shows up at exactly the pixels a model looks at near an object cut off by the frame.

blocks.title: What each border rule fetches for indices outside a 4-pixel row

scenes.caption: The source row has four pixels, values 10, 40, 90, 160 at indices 0 to 3. Interpolation near an edge asks for indices like -1 and 4, and the border rule decides what comes back.

REPLICATE (clamp): the index is clamped into range, so everything to the left reads pixel 0 and everything to the right reads pixel 3. Cheap, and it keeps the edge color, which is usually the least surprising choice for photos.
REFLECT: the row is mirrored with the edge pixel repeated, so -1 reads 0 and -2 reads 1, while 4 reads 3 and 5 reads 2. The fetched values become 40, 10 on the left and 160, 90 on the right.
REFLECT101: mirrored without repeating the edge, so -1 reads 1 and -2 reads 2. This is the rule most convolution libraries default to, because it does not double the edge pixel's weight in a filter.

WRAP takes the index modulo the width, so the left edge reads the right end of the row and the opposite edge bleeds in. CONSTANT, not drawn here, returns a fixed 0 instead, the honest choice when the model must tell that nothing was there.

blocks.md: Border handling is not free precision. A bilinear tap set that straddles the edge mixes real and invented pixels, and the invented part is whatever the rule says. If downstream code needs to know which output pixels are real, carry a validity mask or use a constant border and test for it; do not try to infer it from the pixel values.

blocks.question: Why do warp kernels evaluate the inverse transform rather than the forward one?
options: Because the inverse matrix has fewer coefficients, so it costs fewer FMAs
Because a forward scatter writes conflicting pixels and leaves destination holes, while an inverse gather writes each output exactly once
Because only the inverse map can be combined with interpolation
Because the forward map needs atomics for correctness, and atomics are unavailable in image kernels
blocks.explain: The gather form gives every destination pixel exactly one owning thread: no write conflicts, no holes, coalesced stores. Rounding the 16 pixels of a 30 degree rotated 4x4 forward fills only 12 of its 16 output cells. The inverse matrix is the same size as the forward one, and interpolation works in either direction, so neither of the other reasons holds.

blocks.question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
blocks.explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

lessons.title: Color conversion: a 3x3 matrix per pixel, with the right coefficients

blocks.md:
Color conversion is the simplest operator in the set and the easiest one to get subtly wrong. Each output pixel depends only on the same input pixel, so the kernel is a 3x3 matrix times a 3-vector, nine multiply-adds, no neighbours, no interpolation, no borders.

The content is entirely in the coefficients, and they come from broadcast standards. ITU-R BT.601 defines the luma signal as $E_Y = 0.299 E_R + 0.587 E_G + 0.114 E_B$. ITU-R BT.709, the HD standard, defines it as $0.2126 E_R + 0.7152 E_G + 0.0722 E_B$. Same operation, different weights, because the two standards assume different display primaries.

blocks.title: The RGB to YUV matrix CV-CUDA applies

scenes.caption: The matrix a BGR to YUV conversion applies per pixel. Row Y is the BT.601 luma row; the U and V rows are the color differences (B - Y) and (R - Y) rescaled, which is why their entries sum to zero.
The luma row alone. CV-CUDA's source names it "the standard (NTSC and ITU Rec.601) RGB to luma conversion coefficients", and its float constants R2YF, G2YF, B2YF are 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 exactly.

Swap in BT.709 and only the first row changes, but it changes a lot: green's weight goes from 0.587 to 0.7152 and blue's drops from 0.114 to 0.0722. A grayscale conversion done with the wrong row is wrong everywhere, not just on saturated colors.

blocks.md:
Take one pixel, R = 120, G = 200, B = 60. Under BT.601 the luma is $0.299(120) + 0.587(200) + 0.114(60) = 160.12$, which rounds to 160. Under BT.709 it is $0.2126(120) + 0.7152(200) + 0.0722(60) = 172.88$, which rounds to 173. A 13 level difference out of 255 on an ordinary pixel: visible, and systematic across the whole image.

For 8-bit data the kernels avoid floating point entirely. CV-CUDA stores the luma row as 14-bit fixed point: `R2Y = 4899`, `G2Y = 9617`, `B2Y = 1868`, with a `static_assert(R2Y + G2Y + B2Y == (1 << yuv_shift), "BT.601 luma row must be normalized")`. The three integers sum to exactly 16384, so the matrix cannot drift the overall brightness, and the rounding divide is a shift.

blocks.title: The fixed-point luma path, one pixel

scenes.caption: The three coefficients are the BT.601 weights scaled by 2 to the 14 and rounded to integers. Their sum is 16384 exactly, which a compile-time assertion checks.
Our pixel enters: 4899 x 120 + 9617 x 200 + 1868 x 60. Three integer multiply-adds, all in 32-bit registers, no conversion to float.
The descale adds half of the divisor (8192) and shifts right by 14, which is round-to-nearest on a positive value: (2623360 + 8192) >> 14 = 160.
scenes.output: Y = 160, identical to rounding the float result 160.12

scenes.caption: Had the kernel used the BT.709 row instead, the same pixel would leave as 173. The arithmetic is exact either way: the only question that matters is which standard the data came from.

blocks.title: Luma of four pixels under BT.601 and BT.709

scenes.caption: BT.601 luma for four 8-bit RGB pixels. Nothing about the numbers hints that a convention was chosen.

The same four pixels under BT.709: 173, 182, 145, 178. Pure green moves by 32 levels because its weight changed most, while the sky pixel barely moves. A mismatch is invisible on some content and glaring on other content.

blocks.md: YUV and YCbCr are not the same thing even when the luma row is identical. CV-CUDA's OpenCV-derived code forms $U = (B - Y)\,0.492 + \delta$ and $V = (R - Y)\,0.877 + \delta$, the analog YUV scaling. BT.601 instead renormalizes by 1.402 and 1.772 and then quantizes to studio range, $Y' = \mathrm{int}(219 E_Y + 16)$ and $C_B = \mathrm{int}(224 E_{C_B} + 128)$. Our pixel is U = 78.7 in one convention and Cb = 78 in the other after a completely different route. Check which one a decoder hands you.

Is this operator worth tuning? Count its arithmetic against its traffic. Nine FMAs per pixel, 3 bytes read and 3 bytes written: an arithmetic intensity of 1.5 flops per byte. On the V100 the best practices guide uses as its worked example, peak bandwidth is 898 GB/s, so even at full bandwidth the kernel needs about 1.3 TFLOP/s, a small fraction of what the hardware can do. Color conversion is bandwidth bound with a very large margin.

That sets the budget. A 1920x1080 RGB8 conversion moves 12.44 MB in and out; at the 790 GB/s the guide measures for a well-aligned copy on the same device, the floor is 15.7 microseconds. If your conversion takes 60 microseconds, the matrix is not the problem: the access pattern is, which is lesson one again.

blocks.question: Why does CV-CUDA assert that its three integer luma coefficients sum to exactly 16384?
options: Because 16384 is the largest value that fits in the accumulator
So that the coefficients can be stored in shared memory as 16-bit integers
Because a row that sums to 2 to the 14 maps white to white after the 14-bit shift, so the conversion cannot change overall brightness
Because BT.601 requires exactly 14 fractional bits
blocks.explain: The weights of a luma row sum to 1 in the standard. Scaled by 2 to the 14 and rounded independently they might sum to 16383 or 16385, and every pixel would then come out slightly dark or slightly bright after the shift. The assertion pins the rounding so that R = G = B = 255 gives exactly 255. The shift count is an implementation choice, not something BT.601 specifies.

blocks.question: A grayscale conversion of HD footage uses the 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 row. What is the effect?
options: Any non-neutral pixel's luma is biased, by 13 levels for a mid green-ish pixel and up to about 32 levels for saturated green
No effect, since luma rows differ only by a scale factor
Only saturated reds change, because red's coefficient differs the most
The image becomes brighter overall by a constant offset that can be subtracted out
blocks.explain: The rows are not proportional: green goes from 0.587 to 0.7152 and blue from 0.114 to 0.0722. The error depends on the pixel's hue, so it is neither a constant offset nor confined to one channel. For our four sample pixels the gap ranges from 1 to 32 levels, with green worst because its weight moved most.

lessons.title: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo

blocks.md:
Blur, sharpen and gradient filters are neighbourhood operators: an output pixel is a weighted sum of a window of input pixels. A $k \times k$ window means $k^2$ multiply-adds and, naively, $k^2$ global loads per output pixel. At $k = 9$ that is 81 loads where the data only needs to be read once, and the loads are the expensive part.

Two independent savings are available. The first is **separability**: many useful kernels are an outer product of two 1-D kernels, so the 2-D sum can be done as a row pass followed by a column pass. The Gaussian is the standard example, and CV-CUDA's coefficient generator shows it directly, computing each tap as $\exp(-(x^2/2\sigma_x^2 + y^2/2\sigma_y^2))/(2\pi\sigma_x\sigma_y)$, which factors into a function of $x$ times a function of $y$.

blocks.caption: Separability. The left side costs k squared multiply-adds per pixel, the right side 2k, once the inner sums are reused across rows.

blocks.md:
The arithmetic saving grows with the window: 25 taps become 10 at $k = 5$ (2.5x), 81 become 18 at $k = 9$ (4.5x), 289 become 34 at $k = 17$ (8.5x). But two passes also mean writing and re-reading a full intermediate image, so for a bandwidth-bound 8-bit filter a single tiled 2-D pass can still win. Separability is a win in flops always, and a win in time only when the kernel is large enough or the data type wide enough that flops matter.

The second saving is **tiling**: load each input pixel from global memory once into shared memory, synchronize, then let every thread in the block read its window out of shared memory. The cost is that a block computing a $W \times H$ tile of outputs must load a $(W + k - 1) \times (H + k - 1)$ tile of inputs. The extra ring is the **halo**.

blocks.title: Staging a row-pass tile: 8 groups of outputs, 2 of halo

scenes.caption: The CUDA separable convolution sample uses a 16 x 4 block where each thread produces 8 outputs, so one block owns 128 output columns, shown here as 8 groups of 16. The filter radius is 8, so one extra group on each side covers the window.
First the main data: each thread loads its 8 columns straight from global memory, 16 consecutive columns per group, so every load is one coalesced transaction per warp.
Then the left halo. The sample guards it with a predicate instead of a branch, `(baseX >= -i * ROWS_BLOCKDIM_X) ? d_Src[...] : 0`, so out-of-image columns become zeros without diverging the warp.

Then the right halo, the same way. The block has now loaded 160 columns to produce 128, which is 1.25 loads per output instead of the 17 an untiled 17-tap filter would issue: 13.6x fewer global loads.

A barrier, then every thread reads its 17 taps out of shared memory. The whole staged tile is 4 rows x 160 columns of float = 2560 bytes, well inside the shared-memory budget, and the halo is the only redundancy left.

blocks.caption: Conv2D uses a 16x16 block and, for byte-sized pixels, 8 outputs per thread. The kernel coefficients are staged alongside the pixels, so the window is read from shared memory too.

blocks.prompt: With a 16x16 block and a 9x9 kernel, compare one output per thread against eight outputs per thread. How many input loads per output does the halo cost in each case?
blocks.reveal:
One output per thread: the block owns a 16x16 tile and must load 24x24 = 576 inputs for 256 outputs, which is **2.25 loads per output**.

Eight outputs per thread: the block owns 128x16 and loads 136x24 = 3264 inputs for 2048 outputs, which is **1.59 loads per output**.

The halo is a perimeter, so widening the tile amortizes it. That is why CV-CUDA sets `kOutputs` to 8 for byte-sized pixel types: it is not about occupancy, it is about making the perimeter small relative to the area. At 5x5 the same two configurations give 1.56 and 1.29 loads per output.

scenes.caption: Untiled: every output re-reads its whole window from global memory. 25, 81 and 17 loads per output pixel, most of them hitting data a neighbouring thread also wants.

Tiled, with the production block shapes: 1.29, 1.59 and 1.25 loads per output. All that is left is the halo. In loads that is 19x, 51x and 14x less global traffic, and the 9x9 RGBA8 tile is 13380 bytes, 27 percent of the 48 KB CV-CUDA budgets.

blocks.md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

blocks.question: A 16x16 block computing one output per thread stages a tile for a 9x9 filter. How large is the tile, and how much of it is halo?
options: 16x16 = 256 elements, no halo, because shared memory is indexed per thread
25x25 = 625 elements, of which 369 are halo
24x24 = 576 elements, of which 320 are halo: 2.25 loads per output
32x32 = 1024 elements, rounded up to the warp size
blocks.explain: The tile is (16 + 9 - 1) square = 24x24 = 576 elements for 256 outputs, so 320 halo elements and 2.25 loads per output. The halo is k - 1 = 8 elements across both dimensions together, not k, because a radius-4 window needs 4 extra on each side.

blocks.question: Your 9x9 Gaussian on 8-bit images is already tiled at 1.59 loads per output and measures close to the bandwidth limit. You rewrite it as two separable passes. What should you expect?
options: A 4.5x speedup, matching the reduction from 81 taps to 18
No change, because separability only affects arithmetic and arithmetic is free on a GPU
Possibly slower: the arithmetic drops 4.5x but the two passes add a full intermediate write and read to a kernel that was already bandwidth bound
A 2x speedup, one for each pass
blocks.explain: A bandwidth-bound kernel is paced by bytes, not flops. The single tiled pass moves about 1.59 reads plus 1 write per pixel; two separable passes move roughly 1.06 reads plus 1 write, twice, which is more total traffic. Separability pays when the window is large, when the element type is wide enough that the arithmetic matters, or when the intermediate can be kept on chip.

lessons.title: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one

blocks.md:
Everything so far assumed one big image. Real vision pipelines run many small ones: 32 crops at 224x224, a batch of detections to classify, a video's worth of thumbnails. At that size the operator stops being a bandwidth problem and becomes a launch problem.

Put numbers on it. Resizing a 256x256 RGB8 image down to 224x224 reads 196608 bytes and writes 150528, so 347 kB of traffic. At the 790 GB/s the best practices guide measures for an aligned copy on a V100, the kernel's memory work takes about **0.44 microseconds**. Now compare that with what a launch costs. NVIDIA's CUDA Graphs post measures a short kernel on the same class of device at 2.9 microseconds of execution but 9.6 microseconds per kernel when the host synchronizes after each launch, and 3.8 microseconds when launches are allowed to pipeline. The exposed overhead is roughly 0.9 microseconds pipelined and 6.7 microseconds if you synchronize.

The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

blocks.title: Four images: four launches versus one

scenes.caption: One image, one launch. The host spends time submitting the work, then the kernel runs for 0.44 microseconds. Most of the elapsed time is not the kernel. Simplified model: 0.44 us is a bandwidth floor, and the overheads come from a different kernel.
Four images as four launches, pipelined so the host runs ahead. The GPU still gets only 0.44 microseconds of work per 1.34 microseconds of wall clock: the gaps are the launch cost showing through.

Synchronize after each launch and the overhead is fully exposed: the measured cost per short kernel goes from 3.8 to 9.6 microseconds. Four images now take tens of microseconds, past this lane. Avoid per-image synchronization above all else.

One launch whose grid covers all four images: the overhead is paid once and the GPU runs 1.76 microseconds of back-to-back work. Same bytes, same arithmetic, half the time, and the saving grows with the batch.

blocks.md:
Mechanically the batched kernel is the same kernel with one more grid dimension. CV-CUDA's var-shape resize launches `dim3 linGrid(DivUp(outMaxSize.w, blockSize.x * BILINEAR_NIX), DivUp(outMaxSize.h, blockSize.y), in.numImages())`: x and y tile the largest output in the batch, and **z is the image index**. Each thread reads its own image's width, height and base pointer out of a device-side array of per-image descriptors, so nothing about the batch needs to be uniform.

The same shape appears in Conv2D, whose grid is `DivUp(maxSize.w, ...) x DivUp(maxSize.h, ...) x numImages()`. Once the whole batch is one launch, the overhead is amortized across every image in it.

blocks.title: Total time for N small resizes

scenes.caption: At the pipelined overhead of 0.9 microseconds, per-image launches cost 42.9 microseconds for 32 images while one batched launch costs 15.0: a 2.9x gap that is pure overhead, since both do identical work.

Synchronizing after each image pushes the overhead to 6.7 microseconds and the per-image curve to 228 microseconds for the same 32 images, 11x the batched 20.8. The batched curve barely moves: it pays the overhead once.

Now make the images big enough that each kernel runs 3 microseconds. The two curves nearly converge: batching matters in proportion to how small the per-image kernel is, which is why it is the key technique for small crops and almost irrelevant for 4K frames.

blocks.md:
Variable shapes have one cost worth knowing. Because the grid's x and y dimensions are sized by the largest image, a batch with one big outlier launches blocks for every image as if it were that big, and the blocks that fall outside their own image exit at the bounds check.

For the var-shape bilinear configuration (a 8x32 thread block, 4 output columns per thread), a batch of one 1920x1080 image plus 31 crops of 224x224 launches a 60 x 34 x 32 grid: 65280 blocks, of which only 3559 cover real pixels. 94.5 percent of the blocks start and immediately retire. The same 32 images at a uniform 224x224 launch 1568 blocks with no waste. Empty blocks are cheap compared with a kernel launch, but 18x of them is not free, which is the argument for bucketing a batch by size.

blocks.title: Blocks launched for a batch of 32

scenes.caption: A uniform batch of 32 crops at 224x224 launches a 7 x 7 x 32 grid: 1568 blocks, every one of them doing work.

Add one 1920x1080 image to the batch and the grid is sized by it. The blocks that cover real pixels still number only 3559, but 65280 are launched: the 61721 difference exit at their bounds check. Bucketing by size is what avoids this.

blocks.question: A pipeline resizes 64 crops of 256x256 one at a time, synchronizing after each to check for errors. Measurements show the GPU busy about 6 percent of the time. What is the single best change?
options: Switch the interpolation from bilinear to nearest to halve the arithmetic
Increase the block size so each kernel has more parallelism
Use pinned host memory for the output buffers
Batch all 64 crops into one launch and synchronize once at the end
blocks.explain: At 0.44 microseconds of kernel work against 6.7 microseconds of exposed launch overhead, utilization near 6 percent is exactly what the model predicts. Removing 63 launches and 63 synchronizations is the only change that attacks the dominant term. Interpolation arithmetic and block size are irrelevant when the kernel is not the bottleneck, and pinned memory addresses host transfers, not launch overhead.

blocks.question: In a var-shape batch, the grid's x and y dimensions are sized from the largest image. What follows?
options: Blocks are launched for every image as if it were the largest, so a single outlier makes most blocks exit immediately at the bounds check
Smaller images are padded to the largest size before the kernel runs
The kernel must be launched once per distinct image size
Each image gets its own grid, so there is no waste
blocks.explain: z indexes the image and x and y tile the largest output, so every image's slice of the grid is as wide as the biggest one. For one 1920x1080 image among 31 small crops that is 65280 blocks launched against 3559 useful ones. No padding happens and the launch stays single: the waste is empty blocks, which is why batches are usually bucketed by size.

blocks.question: Which of these pipelines gains the least from batching its image operators?
options: 256 thumbnails at 64x64, resized and color converted
A batch of 48 detection crops at 112x112 being normalized
Two 4K frames per step, each getting a 9x9 blur
A batch of 32 crops at 224x224 being resized to 160x160
blocks.explain: A 9x9 blur on a 4K frame moves tens of megabytes and runs for hundreds of microseconds, so a launch overhead of a few microseconds is a rounding error. The other three all have per-image kernels in the microsecond range or below, where overhead dominates. Batching pays in proportion to how small each per-image kernel is.
